transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-16 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Ravi Shen (CTO - Marigold), Leah Porter (PM), Tomás Ruiz (Platform Eng)

Summary: Quick discovery to understand Marigold's TTFT needs for an internal captioning/summary API, decide between Hosted or Dedicated, and outline a PLG quickstart using free credits.

[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, um, i'll let the team quickly intro.
[00:00:12] Ravi: hi i'm ravi, cto at marigold media labs, we build live captioning + highlights for streaming content.
[00:00:20] Leah: leah here, product manager, exploring options for adding summarization and realtime q&a.
[00:00:27] Tomás: tomás, platform eng, i'll be looking at deploy constraints and network.
[00:00:35] Maya: awesome, and from our side liam and priya are here to cover technical and infra questions, we'll try to cover quickstart time to first token and hosting choices.
[00:00:48] Liam: hi all, quick note — i might jump into latency and benchmark items later.
[00:00:54] Priya: hey team, i'll follow up on security and enterprise integrations.

[00:01:10] Maya: to set expectations — two parallel paths we usually recommend: 1) PLG/self-serve using Redwood Hosted API so you can get to first token fast with free credits, SDKs, streaming; 2) Dedicated/private if you need low predictable latency or strict data residency. today's to figure out which makes sense for marigold.

[00:01:40] Ravi: our main metric is end-to-end latency for live captioning, we need median p95 below 300ms ideally for short utterances, and spikes can be tolerated sometimes but not often. cost is important but latency matters more.
[00:01:58] Leah: timeline is fast — we'd like a pilot within 3 weeks if feasible, product team wants something demoable by month end.

[00:02:10] Maya: great, that aligns with a PLG quickstart. with Hosted you can get a curl or SDK call running in minutes, and we give free credits to test throughput. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) for a simple request is typically under a minute if you follow the quickstart, streaming enabled.

[00:02:34] Tomás: can you clarify "under a minute" — is that setup time, or first token latency? we care about per-request latency.
[00:02:42] Maya: good point — TTFT we mean time from signup to first successful API call, not per-token latency. per-request latency for generation depends on model, size, and sequence len. for hosted smaller quantized variants we see 60-200ms for short completions in the benchmarks, p95 can vary.

[00:03:05] Liam: and to add, continuous streaming with small context and KV caching helps — but for live captioning you might use a specialized model and shorter seqs so latency is better. if you need absolute determinism, Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and lat SLOs.

[00:03:28] Leah: what's the friction to try Hosted first? any blockers for us to validate functionality ASAP?
[00:03:35] Priya: usually none — we hand over quickstart steps: sign up, API key, sample curl and node/python snippets, streaming websocket example, and free credits. we'll also share a small test harness for sending your audio->transcript payloads.

[00:03:58] Ravi: data residency is a big thing — for now our content is user-generated video from EU and US. we need audit logs and encryption at rest, and we use our own KMS for keys. can hosted meet that?
[00:04:12] Priya: hosted supports per-customer retention controls and audit logs; for KMS integrations and customer-managed keys we usually recommend Dedicated or Private (V P C) — there is a hosted KMS offering but if you need HSM level or strict key control, Private is the path.

[00:04:35] Tomás: so hosted is fine for early PLG proof if we pseudonymize or avoid PII, but for production we'll likely need dedicated with KMS.
[00:04:44] Maya: exactly, many customers do hosted for TTFT and early evals, then move to Dedicated or Private for production compliance.

[00:05:00] Leah: you mentioned dedicated — what's the minimum commitment and setup time?
[00:05:06] Liam: Dedicated is reserved capacity, minimum is typically monthly contract depending on GPU type; setup varies — for simple configs we can spin up a dev pool in 2-4 weeks, production with SLA and networking can be 4-8 weeks. if you need an on-prem package that's a separate private deployment timeline.

[00:05:32] Ravi: ok that's slower than our pilot timeline. so plan is hosted quickstart to demo, then evaluate Dedicated for production.

[00:05:40] Tomás: network and VPC details — how do we route traffic? we run in GCP europe-west1.
[00:05:46] Priya: we have regional hosted endpoints; for Dedicated you can have private peering and a V P C option for Private. we'll share the network diagram and peering checklist.

[00:06:05] Maya: any specific throughput numbers for pilot? like qps and avg tokens per request?
[00:06:12] Leah: initial pilot is low qps, maybe 10 concurrent streams peaking at 40, each request ~120 tokens. production could be hundreds qps.

[00:06:23] Liam: that's a good fit for hosted to evaluate. we'll provide a cost estimate ballpark and batching suggestions to reduce unit cost. also quantization options if you care about inference cost.

[00:06:40] Ravi: what about model options, are there Redwood-verified open models, or do you host third-party?
[00:06:48] Maya: we host a catalog of open models plus some Redwood-verified builds. you can pick smaller low-latency variants for streaming and higher quality variants for offline summarization. there are tradeoffs.

[00:07:04] Leah: okay, security again — SOC2 and SSO are musts. do you support SAML/SSO and enterprise audit logs?
[00:07:12] Priya: yes SOC2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and long-term audit log retention are part of our enterprise offering. we'll attach our SOC2 report and an SSO integration guide.

[00:07:28] Tomás: do you offer per-request encryption with our KMS?
[00:07:32] Priya: hosted can do at-rest encryption, but for customer-managed KMS we advise Dedicated/Private. we'll document the options in the security packet.

[00:07:45] Maya: let's talk quickstart steps so you know the TTFT experience — sign up, grab API key, try the example curl, enable streaming if needed. we'll give free credits, and we can pre-provision sandbox tokens for your team to avoid signup friction.

[00:08:05] Leah: pre-provisioned tokens would be great. how long do credits last?
[00:08:09] Maya: usually credits valid 30 days, and we extend them on a case-by-case basis for pilots.

[00:08:18] Ravi: what about SDKs/embeds for node/python, and sample code for streaming websocket?
[00:08:23] Liam: we have official SDKs and a streaming example repo, we'll share the repo link. the websocket handshake and chunking pattern is already in samples.

[00:08:35] Maya: i'll note links in follow-up: quickstart, streaming repo, security pack.

[00:08:50] Tomás: small question on caching — for live streams can you do prefix caching or is that only for text completions?
[00:08:57] Liam: prefix/KV caching is mainly used for chat-like workloads with repeated context; for unique live utterances it's less beneficial but still helps for repeated speaker context. we'll explore options in the benchmark.

[00:09:18] Leah: ok let's briefly go through evaluation criteria — what will we measure in the pilot?
[00:09:24] Maya: TTFT to run first test, per-request latency p50/p95, token cost, quality (WER for transcripts and ROUGE for summaries), and operational fit (SSO, audit, region).

[00:09:38] Ravi: quality metrics interesting — we need a reproducible eval, can you help set that up?
[00:09:44] Liam: absolutely — we'll create a benchmark plan with sample payloads and scoring scripts, can run against Hosted models and later against Dedicated variants.

[00:09:57] Leah: any gotchas for streaming vs chunked transcripts?
[00:10:01] Liam: streaming reduces latency but increases connection churn; chunked batching reduces cost. we'll recommend a hybrid pattern for live captioning.

[00:10:16] Maya: quick note on pricing transparency — we'll send a simple units/cost breakdown and show how batching and quantization affect unit economics.

[00:10:30] Ravi: about competitors — we're also talking to Anthropic and evaluating self-hosted Triton. how do you differentiate?
[00:10:36] Maya: our positioning is production inference ergonomics: predictable serving, rollouts, model variants, and the tooling for cost/latency control. we focus on developer experience and operational SLAs.

[00:10:50] Tomás: is there an easy way to do a smoke test in our staging environment without exposing user data?
[00:10:56] Priya: yes we can provide a sandbox endpoint and guidance for synthetic payloads; also pro-tip, you can pseudonymize traces and still assess latency/throughput.

[00:11:12] Leah: let's capture next steps — sounds like: 1) Redwood sends security pack + quickstart repo + pre-provisioned tokens; 2) Redwood prepares benchmark plan; 3) Marigold shares traffic profile and confirms pilot participants.
[00:11:27] Maya: yep, i'll take action on the docs and tokens. liam will do the benchmark plan.

[00:11:35] Ravi: timeline again — can we get the docs by friday? (2026-06-18)
[00:11:40] Maya: yes that's fine.

[00:11:45] Leah: one more question on logs — what's retention by default?
[00:11:49] Priya: hosted default is 30 days, enterprise can extend retention and export logs to your SIEM.

[00:11:58] Tomás: any specific firewall rules for peering?
[00:12:02] Liam: we'll attach the peering checklist; minimal outbound TLS to our regional endpoints is usually enough for hosted. Dedicated/private require more config.

[00:12:18] Maya: i want to surface an internal note — if you need sub-300ms p95 for every request at scale, we should plan for Dedicated with careful model selection and kernel pathing. for pilot we won't enforce that yet.

[00:12:36] Ravi: ok understood. this is helpful.

[00:12:42] Leah: can you share example latency numbers for small vs medium models?
[00:12:46] Liam: roughly, for small low-latency models p50 is 30-120ms, p95 80-300ms depending on seq len. medium models are larger. we'll include concrete numbers in the benchmark doc.

[00:13:05] Maya: any other concerns?
[00:13:09] Tomás: nothing else now. we'll need the SAML plan later.

[00:13:15] Maya: cool. quick wrap: send security + quickstart + pre-provisioned tokens by 6/18, benchmark plan by 6/21, follow-up deep dive late June.

[00:13:29] Ravi: thanks all.

Action items (as captured):
- Maya: email security pack (SOC2) + network diagram + quickstart repo and pre-provisioned tokens (due 2026-06-18)
- Liam: produce benchmark plan with sample payloads & scoring script (due 2026-06-21)
- Ravi: share traffic profile, preferred region, pilot contacts (due 2026-06-22)

References and links shared:
